newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin aide Chubais insists Yeltsin in command.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin aide Chubais insists Yeltsin in command.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin's chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais, unveiled a new-look Kremlin administration on Wednesday and sent a strong message to manoeuvring rivals that the president was still in command from his hospital room.

Pledging a new openness and accountability on the part of his administration, Chubais told a news conference the keynote of the reforms he has completed since Yeltsin's reelection in July was that the president's orders would be obeyed.
"Officials should not discuss orders but carry them out," said Chubais, the 41-year-old former economic reform supremo who helped engineer Yeltsin's election victory.

He dismissed speculation, which he said was largely the creation of Western media, that Russia has been rudderless since Yeltsin retreated from view shortly before his reelection. The president is preparing for heart surgery in a month or two.

Chubais, who is seen as a key figure in apparent jostling for position among senior officials in Yeltsin's absence, had harsh words for Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed and warned the president's political foes that any jockeying for the succession was premature.

Asked if the business of government was stagnating while Yeltsin was away from his office, Chubais said: "I don't know of a situation when we needed a presidential decision in some difficult, dramatic conflict and we weren't able to get it."
He acknowledged that Yeltsin's limited working time of two to three hours a day was not ideal. Chubais said he had not seen the president since last week.
But he denied suggestions -- partly coming from Lebed -- that he or other officials were using facsimile signatures on decrees to govern without the president's knowledge.
Not a single decision had been rubber-stamped, Chubais said.
Such facsimile signatures were occasionally used on routine, low-level business -- such as congratulating "societies of dog breeders" -- but even then only with Yeltsin's full consent.

Chubais cited the appointment on Thursday of Yuri Baturin, Lebed's predecessor as national security adviser, to head a committee supervising senior army appointments. Lebed objected, but Chubais said the decision was entirely Yeltsin's own.
"Before the president took this decision, he had on his desk detailed arguments from Alexander Ivanovich Lebed, who objected to this decision," Chubais said.

"This decision may not suit some people, but I categorically deny any claim that the mechanism for taking decisions is not understood, that some facsilime was used, which Chubais put in his pocket and used in the dead of night."

Asked if Lebed and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin were jockeying for Yeltsin's succession, Chubais insisted he expected the president to see out his four-year term and that Lebed and the premier were working as part of the same team.

But he added wryly that Chernomyrdin worked hard without seeking the limelight while "we can always turn on the television and find out what Alexander Ivanovich (Lebed) has done recently and what he's planning to do next".

Chubais said of those who were ready for an early election: "Very soon it will be clear this is a false start and those who started quickly will have to return to the starting line under the watchful gaze of the referee -- President Boris Yeltsin."
Chubais is putting regional policy firmly in the domain of the Kremlin administration rather than the government.
He repeated his plan to institute a Soviet-style centralised system for supervising officials and moving around the regions.

Noting the gravity of economic problems, Chubais criticised regional leaders in the Far East for "a profound lack of professionalism" and "gross mistakes" that had contributed to bitter strikes over unpaid wages.
